metadata.title: Launching an AI Product: From Beta to Production

beats.narration_text: Hello, I'm Vineet S.. Launching an A I product is not one day. It is a staged path from a small pilot to full production, and the work continues after launch. Here is how product managers run it.

props.segment: Launching an AI Product: From Beta to Production
props.command: How do I launch an AI product safely, from beta to production?
output: Start small with pilots and beta users
Roll out in stages, with rollback ready

beats.narration_text: An AI launch keeps going, long after launch. Models drift, users surprise you, and providers change their models. The real work is the monitoring, learning and improving that follows.

props.text:
An AI launch
ends on
launch day.

beats.narration_text: Here is the path. Pilot. Beta. A B testing. Staged rollout. Monitoring. Customer feedback. And continuous improvement. Each stage lowers risk before the next one raises exposure.

Start with a pilot: a small group, often internal or friendly customers, with close support. Learn whether the product solves the problem at all. Then widen to a beta with real users. Set clear exit criteria in advance, for example quality scores, error rates, and satisfaction, so the decision is not a feeling.

layers.title: Pilot
layers.sub: A small, friendly group, closely watched

layers.title: Beta
layers.sub: Real users, wider and less supervised

beats.narration_text: Use A B testing to compare the new AI experience against the current one, on the metrics that matter. Then roll out in stages, a few percent of traffic, then more, using feature flags. Watch the numbers at each step, and keep a rollback ready, so you can switch back quickly if something breaks.

props.arcCaption: For example: five percent, then more

beats.narration_text: After launch, monitoring is the product. Track production metrics: answer quality samples, error and fallback rates, latency, cost per request, and safety incidents. Add alerts for sudden changes. Review real conversations regularly, with privacy rules, because dashboards miss problems that people can see.

layers.title: Quality samples
layers.sub: Review real outputs on a schedule

layers.title: Safety incidents
layers.sub: A clear path to escalate and fix

beats.narration_text: Customer feedback closes the loop. Add thumbs and comments, and read support tickets. Turn failures into new test cases. Also plan for model changes. A provider update or your own upgrade can shift behavior, so re-run your evaluation set and roll the change out gradually, just like a feature.

props.caption: Treat a model change as a release

beats.narration_text: Then improve continuously. Review metrics weekly. Fix the biggest failure first. Grow the test set from real problems. Revisit cost and model choice as prices fall. And tell users what improved, because trust grows when people see you listening.

layers.title: Grow the test set
layers.sub: Add real problems as new cases

layers.title: Tell users
layers.sub: Trust grows when they see progress

beats.narration_text: So, launching. Start with pilots and beta. Use A B tests and staged rollouts. Monitor in production. Learn from feedback. And treat every model change like a release.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. I am a product manager launching an AI feature that does this: [describe it]. Draft a launch plan with pilot and beta stages, exit criteria for each, an A/B test design, a staged rollout schedule with rollback triggers, the production metrics and alerts I need, and a process for handling model changes. Then tell me the riskiest assumption in the plan. Pay most attention to the riskiest assumption. Turn it into an explicit exit criterion for your pilot, so you learn it before wider exposure. Pause here and run it on your own product.
